title: Design a Satellite Beam Assignment Algorithm
prompt:
Given Earth-centered 3D coordinates for users on a spherical Earth and for satellites, assign as many users as possible to a satellite and one of four frequencies. Return a mapping from each served user to its satellite and frequency. Each user may be served at most once.

- A satellite can serve at most 32 users.
- At the user, the direction toward the satellite must be within 45 degrees of the outward surface normal.
- At a satellite, beams using the same frequency must be at least 10 degrees apart. Different frequencies may serve closer users.

Some inputs cannot serve every user. Describe an assignment algorithm and an independent feasibility validator, and explain how you trade coverage against a fixed computation budget. A globally optimal assignment is not required.

response.placeholder: Write the visibility and same-frequency conflict predicates, then explain a coverage heuristic and how you validate its output.
response.reference_answer:
## Geometry and feasibility

For user position u and satellite position s, visibility is the angle between u and s - u: it must be at most 45 degrees. The outward normal is u because the Earth is centered at the origin. For two users u and v served by satellite s on the same frequency, compare u - s with v - s: their angle must be at least 10 degrees. These angles are measured at different endpoints. Use normalized dot products and explicit floating-point tolerances near the boundaries.

Build a bipartite visibility graph, then per-satellite conflict edges between candidate users separated by less than 10 degrees. Each satellite may select at most 32 users, colored with four frequencies. A user may occur in at most one satellite assignment.

## Assignment strategy

For small instances, a constraint-programming or integer-programming model can establish optimal coverage. For larger instances, prioritize users with few visible satellites, choose a satellite with available capacity and a feasible frequency, and update conflicts after every assignment. Greedy placement can strand users; bounded local swaps or reassignment improve coverage. Keep the best valid assignment when the computation budget expires. There is no claim that a greedy heuristic reaches the optimum.

## Independent validation

Check user and satellite IDs, frequency membership, unique user assignment, satellite capacity, visibility, and every same-frequency beam pair. Include no-visible-satellite cases, users sharing one direction, capacity saturation, and angles exactly at 45 and 10 degrees. Distinguish physically infeasible users from users left uncovered by the heuristic; a failed greedy choice is not proof of infeasibility.

## Practice scope

The public challenge copy supplies the geometry and capacity above. This is a written algorithm-design exercise based on that assignment; it does not reproduce the original hidden datasets or score thresholds.
